Learning Objectives
Describe the typical presentation of a patient with a benign or malignant bone lesion.
Discuss the workup for bone lesions based on patient presentation.
Describe the typical presentation of a patient with a benign or malignant soft-tissue mass.
Discuss physical examination findings in patients with a benign soft-tissue mass.
Discuss physical examination findings in patients with a malignant soft-tissue mass.
Describe the appropriate workup for concerning soft-tissue masses.

Benign bone conditions (Video 1)
Much more common than malignant bone disease
Developmental processes
Reactive processes (osteomyelitis, stress fractures, bone cysts)
Benign, aggressive tumors (aneurysmal bone cyst, giant cell tumor, chondroblastoma)
Nonneoplastic reactive conditions include hematomas and heterotopic ossification.
Malignant bone conditions
Malignancies that arise from mesenchymal derivatives are called sarcomas.
Approximately 3,260 new bone and joint sarcomas and 12,390 new soft-tissue sarcomas
are diagnosed annually in the United States.
Primary bone sarcoma includes osteogenic sarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and chondrogenic
sarcoma.
Most of these sarcomas are high-grade malignancies with a propensity to metastasize.
Well-differentiated (low-grade) sarcomas are associated with a risk of metastasis in less
than 10% of patients.
Moderately differentiated (intermediate grade) sarcomas are associated with a risk of
metastasis in 10% to 30% of patients.
High-grade undifferentiated sarcomas are associated with a risk of metastasis in more
than 30% of patients.
Bone malignancies that are not sarcomas include metastatic bone disease, multiple
myeloma, and lymphoma.
Soft-tissue masses (Video 2)
Most common soft-tissue tumors
Benign: lipoma, myxoma, hemangioma, fibromatosis, schwannoma, juxta-articular cysts
Malignant: undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (previously called malignant fibrous
histiocytoma), liposarcoma, synovial sarcoma

Overview
Benign bone conditions, which are much more common than malignant bone tumors,
have a broad, differential diagnosis and generally are grouped into three categories.
Reactive processes include osteomyelitis, stress fractures, and bone cysts, many of
which can be managed via close observation. Osteomyelitis typically requires surgical
management, especially in the presence of sequestrum. Nonneoplastic reactive
conditions, such as subperiosteal hematoma or heterotopic ossification, may be
observed. Benign, aggressive bone tumors, such as aneurysmal bone cysts, giant cell
tumor of bone, and chondroblastoma, typically require surgical management to remove
the tumor.
Malignant bone conditions frequently are diagnosed by orthopedic surgeons. These
include bone sarcoma, metastatic disease, and myeloma and lymphoma of bone.
Soft-tissue masses may be benign or malignant in nature. Most soft-tissue masses are
benign; however, surgeons should ensure the mass is benign before proceeding with
surgical management. Unplanned excision of malignant soft-tissue masses without
consideration of appropriate diagnosis, management, and margin may result in morbid
consequences.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Bone Tumors
Age is a crucial factor in developing a differential diagnosis1 (Resource 1).

Surgeons must determine the manner in which the lesion discovered. Incidentally found
lesions are unlikely to be malignant; however, painful lesions are more concerning.
Location of the lesion (epiphyseal, metaphyseal, diaphyseal; eccentric, concentric)
Current symptoms (pain, rate of growth, skin changes, presence of mass)
Pain
Destructive bone tumors
Pain is intermittent and progresses to constant pain that does not respond to NSAIDs or
weak narcotic medications.
Pain with weight-bearing activity suggests weakening of the bone involved.
A common presentation is severe pain that occurs at rest and with activity.
Night pain often is present (must be carefully elicited, especially if the patient is a child).
Pain that wakes the patient up at night
Any requirement for analgesic medication at night (eg, aspirin, NSAIDs, acetaminophen)
Presence of a mass: assess if noticed in relation to other symptoms and rate of growth; a
bone tumor may have an associated soft-tissue mass or swelling.
Relevant personal or family history
Personal or family history of cancer
History of multiple enchondromatosis or multiple hereditary exostoses
History of known genetic abnormality
Exposure (eg, irradiation)
History of infection or trauma (eg, myositis ossificans)
Prior surgery

Bone Tumors
The patient history is critical in developing a differential diagnosis for bone tumors.
Patient age is readily accessible and is the first determinate in narrowing the differential
diagnosis. Metastatic carcinoma typically does not occur in individuals who are aged 16
years. Conversely, primary osteosarcoma or Ewing sarcoma is exceedingly rare in
individuals older than 40 years. Incidentally found lesions are rarely of any real
importance. Pain is an especially crucial factor in determining next steps in
management. Bone tumors that are not painful often are benign in nature and may
require no more than close observation. Pain with weight-bearing activity suggests that
the bone is weakened and, therefore, the condition should be investigated and managed

carefully and quickly. Although family history should be obtained for new patients, it may
not prove useful. However, a patient’s personal history may be useful in investigating a
newly found bone tumor and may help narrow the differential diagnosis.
Soft-Tissue Tumors 
Age is a crucial factor in developing differential diagnoses2 (Resource 2).
Consistency of mass
Benign soft-tissue masses typically are soft and mobile.
Malignant soft-tissue masses typically are firm in nature and often are fixed to surrounding
structures.
Some malignant masses may be soft, and some benign masses may be firm; therefore,
consistency should not be used in isolation to determine diagnosis.
Location of mass
Masses that are superficial to fascia often are found before they become large because of
their location. These may be benign or malignant.
Deep soft-tissue masses may grow to a large size before they are detected. Large, deep soft-
tissue masses are more concerning for malignancy and should be evaluated with care.
Juxta-articular masses may be benign or malignant, and some juxta-articular cysts may
become very large.
Presenting symptoms
Pain
Patients with benign soft-tissue tumors commonly present without pain.
Patients with malignant soft-tissue tumors often present without pain unless rapid growth
or impingement on neural structures is present.
Painful soft-tissue masses include nerve sheath tumors, hemangioma, angiolipoma,
infection. and fibromatosis.
A rapidly growing soft-tissue mass may suggest malignancy or infection. Some malignant soft-
tissue tumors grow slowly (eg, synovial sarcoma, epithelioid sarcoma).
Relevant personal and family history
Personal or family history of cancer
Exposure (eg, irradiation)
History of known genetic abnormality
History of infection or trauma (eg, hematoma, seroma)

Prior surgery

Soft-Tissue Tumors
Similar to the diagnosis of bone tumors, patient age is helpful in the diagnosis of soft-
tissue tumors. Soft-tissue masses in young individuals are often, but not always, benign.
Growth over time is very useful in diagnosis. Typically, malignancies grow and change
over time. A soft-tissue mass that has been present for 15 years and is not growing is
very unlikely to be of importance. Pain also is very useful in narrowing the differential
diagnosis. Painful soft-tissue masses include nerve sheath tumor, hemangioma,
angiolipoma, and fibromatosis. Soft-tissue sarcoma often presents as a painless,
enlarging mass. Pain may occur in patients with a large soft-tissue sarcoma begins to
impinge on neurovascular structures. Personal history, especially any history of cancer,
is useful in adding to the diagnostic strategy. Patients with a history of high-dose
radiation therapy are at risk for radiation-associated sarcoma. Masses that are deep to
fascia, fixed to surrounding structures, greater than 5 cm, and firm are concerning for
malignancy and should be evaluated and managed carefully.
Physical Examination
Bone Tumors
Mass—Patients with bone tumors present with a hard, fixed mass adjacent to the bone lesion
that occasionally is tender on deep palpation.
Range of motion—The joint adjacent to a bone tumor often has diminished range of motion.
Muscle atrophy: common, adjacent to painful lesion
Lymphadenopathy—Lymph nodes may be enlarged because of infection or metastasis. This is
rare but not impossible in patients with a bone lesion.
Pathologic fractures
Fractures through a bone lesion occur in 5% to 10% of patients.
A history of antecedent pain is common.
Pathologic fractures generally occur with minor trauma or after activities of daily living.

9/3/26, 5:50 PM

7/17


Bone Tumors
Physical examination is important in any visit to the orthopedic surgeon. Bone tumors
may present in combination with an associated soft-tissue mass. Muscle atrophy may be
present, especially in patients with long-standing painful lesions in whom weight bearing
has been restricted. Lymphadenopathy is rare in patients with a malignant bone lesion
but should always be examined. Range of motion of the affected side should be
examined and compared with that of the contralateral side because some periarticular
bone tumors may considerably alter joint range of motion. Gait patterns also should be
examined to identify a limp.
Soft-Tissue Tumors
Benign soft-tissue masses tend to be soft, mobile, and superficial, with slow or no growth.
Malignant soft-tissue masses tend to be firm, fixed to surrounding structures, often deep to
fascia, and likely growing at various rates.
Large masses may lead to extremity swelling and vascular or neurologic compressive
symptoms.
Overlying skin changes (erythema, ecchymosis, peau d’orange)
Lymphadenopathy—Lymph nodes may be enlarged because of infection or metastatic spread.
Range of motion: The joint adjacent to a large, deep soft-tissue mass occasionally has
diminished range of motion.
Painful, tender soft-tissue masses include angiolipoma, desmoid (fibromatosis), and nerve
sheath tumors.
Patients with a nerve sheath tumor often have positive Tinel sign.
Ganglions may transilluminate.

Soft-Tissue Tumors
Physical examination of patients with a soft-tissue mass should begin with examination
of the mass itself. The mass should be measured using a measuring tape to document
size. If an extremity lesion is present, the involved extremity should be compared with

8/17

the contralateral extremity. The lesion should be classified as dermal, subdermal, or
subfascial in nature via direct palpation of the mass. Mild tenderness is a nonspecific
finding; however, very painful lesions can help narrow the differential diagnosis. Patients
with a nerve sheath tumor may have a positive Tinel sign. Physical examination findings
of masses that are superficial, less than 3 cm in size, soft, and freely mobile may be
reassuring for a benign process.
Imaging Studies
Bone Tumors
Radiography
Plain radiographs
Primary bone lesion
Plain radiographs alone (two planes) often are sufficient for benign bone lesions.
Cortices should be inspected for bone destruction.
Lesion should be assessed for mineralization.
Rings/stipples suggest a cartilage lesion.
Cloudlike lesions suggest bone formation.
Periosteal reaction should be evaluated.

Radiography
All bone tumors should be evaluated via plain radiographs, which are simple, readily
obtainable, cheap, and the single best imaging modality to aid in the diagnosis of benign
or malignant bone tumors. Cortices should be inspected for thinning. Tumors should be
inspected for matrix pattern (chondroid, osteoid, or ground glass). Periosteal reaction
should be assessed and determined to be benign (unilamellar, smooth, organized) or
malignant (sunburst, hair-on-end appearance, or multilamellar and disorganized).
Computed Tomography

Determines the mineral distribution in normal and abnormal bone
Can show more detail of osseous structure not identified on MRI (endosteal scalloping in low-
grade chondrosarcoma)
Helpful in evaluating pelvic and spine lesions
Thin-cut CT should be ordered if osteoid osteoma is suspected.
Preferred imaging modality for workup of skeletal lesions of unknown origin
CT chest/abdomen/pelvis alone will provide a diagnosis in more than 70% of patients with
metastatic disease3 (Resource 3)

Computed Tomography
To evaluate the internal characteristics of the bone with the lesion, CT may be very
useful. CT affords better views of bony architecture than MRI. Specifically, CT may be
nearly diagnostic for low-grade chondrosarcoma in patients with a painful bony lesion
with a chondroid appearance on plain radiographs because CT may show endosteal
scalloping in great detail. CT also may be quite useful for patients with a lesion who have
a history and radiographs consistent with osteoid osteomas because it may help identify
the cortical nature and central nidus that is classic for these lesions. CT also is very useful
for evaluating deeper bony structures, such as pelvic and spine lesions.
A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis can identify the primary site of disease in
more than 70% of patients with a skeletal lesion of an unknown primary source.3 The
entire workup (patient history; physical examination; CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis;
whole body bone scan; serum protein electrophoresis; urine protein electrophoresis;
and biopsy) will identify approximately 85% of primary sites of disease. A CT scan of the
chest also is required in patients diagnosed with bone sarcoma because the chest is the
most common site of metastatic disease.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Sensitive and specific for detecting bone marrow involvement
Defines anatomic features (T1-weighted MRI)
Helpful in evaluating pelvic and spine bone lesions
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:50 PM
AAOS | Presentation and Evaluation of Bone and Soft-Tissue Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004037
10/17

Can help identify skip lesions in bone

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may aid in the diagnosis of bone tumors and in determining the extent of marrow
involvement. MRI should include the entire bone involved to evaluate for potential skip
metastasis. In patients with a soft-tissue mass associated with a bone lesion, MRI also is
very useful to determine the extent of disease and help identify relevant anatomy
adjacent to the soft-tissue mass.
Bone Scintigraphy
Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy
Technetium-99m forms chemical adducts to sites of new bone formation.
Detects multiple sites of bone involvement or skip metastases
Very sensitive but not specific
High false-negative rate in multiple myeloma and occasionally in very osteolytic bone
metastasis, such as renal cell carcinoma

Bone Scintigraphy
Bone scintigraphy can be performed to evaluate the entire skeleton in a single scan and
is part of the workup for various diseases. Bone scintigraphy requires positive
osteoblastic function. Bone scintigraphy is indicated for all primary tumors of bone (eg,
osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma) to evaluate the entire skeleton. It also is useful for
determining the extent of bony disease in patients with metastatic carcinoma. Utility is
limited in patients with myeloma because of the lack osteoblastic activity in as many as
30% of patients; skeletal survey usually is preferred in patients with this diagnosis.
Positron Emission Tomography
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:50 PM
AAOS | Presentation and Evaluation of Bone and Soft-Tissue Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004037
11/17

Currently, positron emission tomography (PET) is not the preferred imaging modality for the
work up of sarcoma.
May be performed in some patients with metastases
Useful for sarcoma subtypes that tend to metastasize through the lymphatic system

Positron Emission Tomography
PET typically is not used in the primary diagnosis of bone tumors but may be used for
certain diagnoses, such as lung and breast cancer, to define disease sites that may
otherwise be overlooked.
Other Studies
Skeletal survey typically is used as an alternative to bone scintigraphy in patients with
myeloma.
Soft-Tissue Tumors
Radiography
Plain radiographs: not particularly useful for soft-tissue masses but are readily available,
cheap, and easily obtained
Primary soft-tissue lesions
Synovial sarcomas: scattered calcifications are observed in 30%.
Myositis ossificans: peripheral mineralization
Hemangiomas: phleboliths in soft tissue; may observe chronic benign appearing changes in
adjacent bone.
Lipomas: radiolucent on plain radiographs

Radiography
Plain radiographs are not very useful for soft-tissue masses; however, they occasionally
may aid in diagnosis. Deep lipomatous tumors will appear radiolucent on plain
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:50 PM
AAOS | Presentation and Evaluation of Bone and Soft-Tissue Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004037
12/17

radiographs. Several soft-tissue masses, including synovial sarcoma, hemangioma, and
myositis ossificans, may show calcification.
Ultrasonography
Quick, inexpensive, and can be performed at bedside for lesions more consistent with benign
processes, such as juxta-articular cysts
Useful if concern for vascular neoplasms, such as hemangioma or avascular malformation,
exists

Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography is quick, easy, and relatively inexpensive. Often, ultrasonography can
be performed in the office and immediately aid in diagnosis. Ultrasonography is useful
for identifying juxta-articular cysts and vascular neoplasms. Because of the ability of
ultrasonography to evaluate for vascular flow, it is a useful imaging modality for patients
in whom vascular masses are being considered.
Computed Tomography
Typically performed in patients with a soft-tissue tumor for staging of the lungs and/or
abdomen and pelvis for concerning soft-tissue masses
Used in follow-up surveillance in patients with soft-tissue sarcoma
Can be used for mass clarification in patients unable to undergo MRI (eg, pacemaker, spinal
stimulator)

Computed Tomography
CT is useful for malignant soft-tissue masses, mainly for staging purposes. Soft-tissue
sarcoma can metastasize to various tissues, depending on the subtype of sarcoma, most
typically the lungs. CT also can be performed in patients who cannot otherwise undergo

13/17

MRI of a soft-tissue mass (eg, patients with implantable devices that are not MRI
compatible). CT also aids in evaluating the ossification patterns of tumors, in which
malignant tumors commonly ossify centrally and benign tumors (myositis ossificans)
ossify peripherally.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Preferred for work up of soft-tissue masses
Defines anatomic features (T1-weighted MRI)
Determinate masses: performed if the nature of lesion can be determined definitively via
analysis of MRI (eg, lipoma, ganglion cyst, hemangioma, muscle injury); these can be
definitively managed without biopsy.
Indeterminate masses: performed if the nature of lesion cannot be determined by analysis of
MRI; these require a biopsy before definitive management.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is preferred imaging modality for soft tissues. Lipoma, ganglion cysts, and
hemangioma often can be diagnosed via MRI. In addition, MRI is a very sensitive imaging
modality that can narrow the differential diagnosis for other masses, shows relevant
anatomic structures, and aids in biopsy and surgical planning. The main disadvantage of
MRI is cost. In addition, some patients may have implanted devices, such as pacemakers,
deep brain stimulators, and spinal stimulators that are not MRI compatible.
Positron Emission Tomography
Currently, PET for staging is evolving. As of 2021, some centers are using PET routinely for
staging, whereas other centers are using PET in selective instances.
Useful for sarcoma subtypes that tend to metastasize through the lymphatic system

Positron Emission Tomography
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:50 PM
AAOS | Presentation and Evaluation of Bone and Soft-Tissue Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004037
14/17

PET is a useful imaging modality for certain soft-tissue sarcomas; however, it currently is
not recommended for the work up of all soft-tissue sarcoma. Synovial sarcoma,
epithelioid sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, clear-cell sarcoma, and angiosarcoma have
the propensity to metastasize through lymphatics and, therefore, can be monitored
closely via PET.
Management
Surgical Management
Indications
Biopsy
Biopsy is a key step in the evaluation and treatment of patients with bone or soft-tissue
lesions.3
The complication rate associated with biopsy is 2 to 12 times greater if biopsy is performed
at a referring institution rather than at the treating institution.
Requires a highly specialized pathologist to interpret the results correctly
Open biopsy and core needle biopsy are preferred.
Fine-needle aspiration has limited role in sarcoma.
Should not be performed by referring physicians who are unsure or would not plan to
manage the diagnosis

Indications
Biopsy requires specialized expertise, surgically and pathologically, to make an accurate
diagnosis. If concern exists that the mass being biopsied may represent a primary bony
or soft-tissue malignancy or if diagnosis is unclear after workup, patients are best served
by undergoing biopsy at the ultimate treating institution.
